def: A fixed, versioned collection of inputs, each with a reference or rubric, used to score a system the same way every time.
When a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure, because systems learn to raise the proxy without improving the real goal.
Precision is the share of what the system flagged that was right; recall is the share of what existed that the system found. F1 is their harmonic mean.
A metric that scores 1 when the normalised output equals the normalised reference and 0 otherwise.
F1 computed over the words shared by an answer and its reference, giving partial credit for overlap but ignoring word order and meaning.
Using a language model with a rubric to grade or compare outputs when no single reference answer exists.
Agreement between two raters corrected for chance: kappa = (observed - expected) / (1 - expected).
A judge's tendency to prefer the answer shown first (or second) regardless of quality, controlled by judging both orders.
The typical sampling wobble of a measured statistic; for a pass rate it is the square root of p(1-p)/n.
A range computed from data that would contain the true value in a stated share (such as 95%) of repeated experiments.
The probability of seeing a difference at least as large as observed if the systems were truly identical; not the probability that the null is true.
The probability that a test detects a real effect of a given size; sample size is chosen to reach about 80%.
A metric computed on a subset of the eval set defined by an input property such as language or topic, revealing weak groups the average hides.
An experiment that randomly assigns real users to the current system or a candidate and compares an outcome metric.
A metric such as latency, cost or complaint rate that must not get worse while the primary metric is improved.
A traffic split that differs from the configured one by more than chance allows, signalling a bug that invalidates the experiment.
A drift measure, the sum over buckets of (actual share - expected share) times the log of their ratio; above about 0.25 means a major shift.
A reversal where one system wins within every slice yet loses overall because the groups have different slice mixes.
When strong models score near a benchmark's achievable ceiling, so differences between them fall within noise and the benchmark stops separating them.
Test items, their answers or close paraphrases appearing in a model's training data, which inflates its score with recall rather than skill.
A model of pairwise comparisons in which the probability that one item beats another depends only on the difference of their strengths; used to fit arena ratings.
Adding style features such as answer length and markdown counts to an arena's rating regression so model ratings reflect preference beyond presentation.
Evaluating models across many scenarios and several metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, efficiency and more) so weaknesses cannot hide behind one score.
A way of working in which every change is judged by evaluations that run the same way each time, with evaluators written for failures observed in real outputs.
The tendency for evaluation criteria to change as people grade outputs, because seeing outputs reshapes what they consider good or bad.
Eval cases the system already passes and must keep passing, expected near 100%, run on every change.
An automated CI check that blocks a change when evaluation results fall below a threshold or drop relative to the baseline by more than noise allows.
Refusing an acceptable request because it superficially resembles a harmful one; also called exaggerated safety.
Effort to draw out a model's maximum capability during evaluation, through prompting, tools, many attempts or fine-tuning, so the result is an upper bound rather than typical behaviour.
